qt: to the Commission Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN) Subject:

On 9 September 2026, the Commission proposed an EU-wide regulatory framework to regulate the housing market: the Affordable Housing Act. Although the Commission itself says that an insufficient supply of housing is the primary catalyst for housing shortages, the proposal specifically includes the regulation of short-term rentals, second homes and vacant properties. The Zentrale Immobilien Ausschuss (Central Real Estate Committee) criticises the proposal for tackling the wrong issues and calls for better investment conditions, additional construction capacity and a greater focus on new building new housing1. The Computer & Communications Industry Association Europe has also warned against excessive regulation of short-term rentals and disproportionate restrictions2. At the same time, housing policy is fundamentally a national competence belonging to Member States and this is therefore a further attempt by the Commission to broaden its competences. 1.

What is the empirical basis for the Commission to expect the regulation of short-term rentals to significantly reduce housing shortages, and how many dwellings will become available in practice as a result?
How will the Commission ensure that additional regulatory requirements do not hamper investment in housing and further reduce the supply of housing?

On what basis of competence under EU law does the Commission base the proposed legal framework, and how does it justify its view that the subject matter falls within the scope of internal market competence rather than the national remit of housing policy?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.11.2026) The proposed Regulation1 and the Recommendation2 form part of implementing the European Affordable Housing Plan3. The Plan recognised that increasing supply is essential to addressing the housing crisis. The impact assessment4 showed that short-term rentals activity can reduce housing availability for long-term residential use and increase prices and rents in constrained local markets. Effects vary by location. As the proposal neither imposes restrictions nor requires their adoption, no reliable Union-wide estimate can be given; outcomes depend on local measures and market responses. The Regulation aims to improve legal certainty through clearer conditions for housing restrictions, including necessity, proportionality, territorial targeting, less restrictive alternatives and review. The Recommendation addresses increasing supply using levers under Member States’ control, including better mobilisation of land; faster planning, permitting, and construction; making better use of the existing building stock; expanding affordable, social and student housing; and mobilising public and private investment. The legal basis for the proposed Regulation is Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Housing policy remains primarily a Member State responsibility. The proposal establishes common conditions for assessing certain restrictions that may affect freedom of establishment, the freedom to provide services and free movement of capital. Where they do, those restrictions are already subject to applicable Union law. It does not confer new powers to restrict housing activities or harmonise substantive housing policy choices.
